§. 4.
*Appellatio ad Concilium Generale.*

Vaticana jam parabantur fulmina: Noaillius ab ipso Cardinalium Collegio purpura indignus censebatur. Nihilominus datum tempus adhuc resipiscendi, ex spe, quam ostenderant Opponentes confecto quodam doctrinæ schemate, quod cum ab acceptantibus probatum non fuit, scriptum eis trium columnarum, Janseniano illi olim simile obtulerunt, in quarum media ipsæ propositiones Quesnelli, ex una parte sensus obvius, ex altera alius quispiam Catholicus, vel certe excusationis patiens

 That you enjoy an excellent republic, I rejoice more than for my own sake. For since the greatest part of my life has been spent, there can be nothing that I might long enjoy. But your era, which is on a better course, looks to the future for many things which it may rightly promise itself by entrusting the magistracies. If, however, there is anything in which I can serve the fatherland, I will not only take up all labors bravely for it, but I will also bear all annoyances and anxieties with an equal mind, and I will consider myself to have received enough fruit from my labors and studies if I leave your republic, which I hold to be most excellent and most ample, to your descendants along with you. If, however, it does not turn out by my service, I will rejoice that the greatest and most wise men are found in your city, who, by the best laws and most wise institutions, can protect the fatherland. I, however, desire more leisure than business for my old age. You, who are occupied in adorning and enriching it, will consider with your wisdom what is fitting for the republic. The first is a certain writing sent by Quesnel himself to a certain priest, who, having finally wiped away the mist of errors and being returned to himself and to the Church, produced it. They were rules comprised in 12 articles, which his followers were to use in conversation among themselves and with various kinds of men. The sum of it was almost this: Union and concord; fidelity to the secret; circumspection in speech according to the various conditions of men; ambiguity in various chapters of Religion; he wanted it to be said that Christ is present in the Eucharist, not only by faith or figure, as the heterodox say, but neither by transubstantiation, nor substantially or really, as the Catholics say: how then? in an imperceptible way. In the Sacrament of Penance, they would urge the insufficiency of attrition and the necessity of perfect contrition. They would openly attack sufficient grace, the liberty of indifference, and merits, sometimes directly and sometimes through the maze of words, so that an exit might be open for the pressured: let them exalt only victorious grace: and so many other things.
